summary: Redefines how the ECN field in the IP header is handled when entering and leaving an IP-in-IP tunnel. It updates RFC 3168 and RFC 4301 so that tunnels in IPv4 and IPv6 behave consistently, with new behaviors on exit.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6040 explains how IP tunnels should carry Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) markings from a packet's inner header to its outer header and back. The rules help preserve congestion information across different kinds of tunnels and allow two congestion severity levels to be distinguished.

questions: how does ecn work in ip-in-ip tunnels
what is ecn normal mode and compatibility mode
what happens to not-ect packets with ce in the outer header
subtitle: Consistent rules for carrying congestion markings through IP-in-IP tunnels.

tldr.problem: Tunnels can hide congestion markings because routers mark the outer IP header, which is removed at the tunnel exit. Earlier IPv4 and IPv6 tunnel rules differed and restricted which markings could pass through.
tldr.mechanism: At tunnel entry, normal mode copies the incoming ECN field to the outer header; compatibility mode clears the outer field to Not-ECT. At exit, one rule combines the inner and outer values, and drops a Not-ECT inner packet if the outer value is CE.
tldr.outcome: The rules allow an extra congestion severity level to pass through and harmonize IP-in-IP tunnel behavior. RFC 6040 updates RFC 3168, RFC 4301 and RFC 4774, and is updated by RFC 9601.

today: RFC 6040 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2010. It updates RFC 3168, RFC 4301 and RFC 4774, and has been updated by RFC 9601.

sections.title: Why Congestion Markings Need Tunnel Rules
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets a forwarding device mark packets to report congestion instead of dropping them. A tunnel adds an outer IP header around the packet. A router inside the tunnel sees and marks that outer header, so the tunnel exit must combine the inner and outer ECN fields when it removes the outer header.

RFC 3168 and RFC 4301 had different encapsulation rules, and their exit rules restricted how much of the ECN field could be propagated. RFC 6040 adds behavior for previously unused combinations so that tunnels can carry four states of congestion signaling, including two severity levels.

The document covers ECN processing at IP-in-IP tunnel endpoints, whether the tunnel uses IPsec or not, and whether the inner and outer headers use IPv4 or IPv6. It does not change congestion-marking algorithms or the response to congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel's outer header can receive a congestion mark while the packet travels inside it. These rules tell the tunnel exit how to preserve that mark when it removes the outer header.

sections.title: The Four ECN Values
sections.content:
The IP header's ECN field has four codepoints. 00 is Not-ECT, for a transport that is not ECN-capable. 01 is ECT(1), 10 is ECT(0), and both indicate an ECN-capable transport. 11 is CE, meaning congestion experienced.

The RFC calls the endpoint that adds an outer header the encapsulator or tunnel ingress. The endpoint that removes it is the decapsulator or tunnel egress. The original packet header is the inner header; after removal, the egress constructs the outgoing header by combining values from the inner and outer headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The ECN field can say that ECN is unavailable, that the transport can use ECN, or that congestion was experienced. The tunnel entrance adds an outer header, and the exit combines its value with the inner header.

sections.title: How the Earlier Tunnel Rules Differed
sections.content:
At entry, RFC 4301 copied the incoming ECN field into the new outer header. RFC 3168 full-functionality mode instead reset an incoming CE value to ECT(0). RFC 3168 also defined a limited-functionality mode that set the outer field to Not-ECT, so congestion had to be signaled by dropping packets rather than marking them.

At exit, the earlier rules generally ignored the outer header when the inner value was Not-ECT. Otherwise, an outer CE became CE in the outgoing header; if the outer value was not CE, the inner value was used. The outer ECT(0) and ECT(1) values were not preserved as separate signals.

These different rules made the result depend on the tunnel type and prevented the ECN field from carrying two different congestion severity levels consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: Older tunnels copied, changed or ignored congestion marks in different ways. Their exit rules also discarded distinctions between the two ECN-capable values.

sections.title: Tunnel Entry: Normal and Compatibility Modes
sections.content:
The tunnel ingress must implement normal mode. In normal mode, it copies the incoming two-bit ECN field to the outer IP header and leaves the inner header unchanged. Compatibility mode instead clears the outer field to Not-ECT, matching the limited-functionality behavior needed for older egresses that do not propagate ECN.

If an ingress may connect to a legacy egress, it must also implement compatibility mode. During dynamic discovery of an egress, it must use compatibility mode until the egress indicates support for ECN propagation. If support is confirmed, it can switch to normal mode. An ingress that claims compliance must not permanently disable ECN processing.

Compatibility mode is optional when the ingress will never be paired with a legacy egress. The RFC says normal mode should be used when the egress is known to propagate ECN.
sections.plainLanguage: When the exit supports ECN, the entrance copies the packet's marking into the outer header. While checking whether an older exit can handle ECN, the entrance clears that outer marking instead.

sections.title: Tunnel Exit: Combine the Inner and Outer Values
sections.content:
The egress uses one decapsulation rule. If the inner field is Not-ECT, the egress must not pass another ECN value to the transport. It drops the packet when the outer field is CE; for any other outer value, it forwards the packet with Not-ECT.

For an ECN-capable inner packet, the outgoing field must carry the more severe of the inner and outer values. The RFC ranks them from most to least severe as CE, ECT(1), ECT(0), and Not-ECT. This lets a scheme give ECT(1) a higher congestion severity than ECT(0).

Some inner and outer combinations have not been used by current or earlier tunnel specifications. The egress should log these combinations and may raise an alarm. Alarms should be rate-limited, and implementations must allow logging or alarms to be suppressed.
sections.plainLanguage: For an ECN-capable packet, the exit keeps the more severe of the inner and outer markings. If a Not-ECT packet has a CE mark outside, the exit drops it because its transport cannot use that signal.

sections.title: Updates and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 6040 changes RFC 3168 and RFC 4301 exit processing for combinations that had not been used by earlier RFC tunnel rules. Existing combinations keep their previous outputs. An RFC 4301 IPsec ingress already copies the ECN field in the way normal mode requires.

The change to an RFC 3168 ingress is called black-box backward compatible by the RFC: packets leaving the tunnel are unchanged, although a CE value copied into the outer header can now be seen inside the tunnel. Compatibility mode retains the earlier limited-functionality behavior when the ingress might meet an older egress.

A compliant egress can interoperate with earlier tunnel ingress behavior without a separate decapsulation mode. Operators wanting two congestion severity levels can require their tunnel endpoints to follow the new rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing tunnel combinations keep their old results. The new rules add behavior for combinations that older specifications had not used, while providing an entry mode for older tunnel exits.

sections.title: The Security Trade-off
sections.content:
ECN is a mutable IP header field and cannot be protected by IPsec's integrity mechanisms. Copying ECN through a tunnel can therefore create a small covert channel: a sender or a device along the tunnel can change values to send information.

The RFC weighs that information-security risk against traffic security. If congestion marks disappear, it becomes harder to monitor congestion and make senders respond. It treats the bandwidth of the two-bit ECN field as a manageable risk and accepts propagation so that congestion information is not lost.

The document also notes that tunnels crossing the boundaries of a Diffserv region may expose alternate ECN meanings, and that ECN nonce coverage is not perfect. It advises avoiding alternate tunnelling rules where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Copying ECN can carry a small hidden signal, but blocking the marks can hide congestion. The RFC treats that limited information channel as an acceptable trade-off for preserving congestion signals.
